title: Direct inhibitory inputs had shorter onset delays than excitatory inputs at shared targets in selected mouse cortical slices
abstract: We compared direct excitatory and inhibitory input delays at the same recorded target cell in Allen Synaptic Physiology r2.1. We used detected connections with a passed response fit and cell-body distance at most 500 micrometres. In mouse visual cortex, 74 targets from 64 inferred animals gave a mean inhibitory minus excitatory onset delay of -0.585 ms. Its nominal 97.5% donor bootstrap interval was -0.836 to -0.351 ms. A check that kept input pairs with distance differences at most 25 micrometres gave -0.321 ms in 29 animals, with an interval of -0.576 to -0.051 ms. Human temporal cortex had 11 targets from seven inferred donors. Its estimate was 1.034 ms, with an interval of -0.167 to 2.296 ms. The human result remains uncertain. This is a comparison of direct inputs from separately stimulated sources. It does not measure a feedforward inhibitory relay or response jitter. Sparse slice samples, source cell composition, fitted onset values, and inferred donor labels limit the result.

display.caption: Direct inhibitory minus excitatory input delay at shared targets. Blue marks show donor-weighted means and nominal 97.5% donor bootstrap intervals. Gray marks show donor contrasts. The first row is primary. Other rows are sensitivity checks. The human inhibitory-target row has one donor and no interval.

citations.reason: Source study of local cortical connectivity and synaptic physiology.
A feedforward inhibitory relay can constrain integration time. The present direct-input contrast does not measure that relay.
Uses inferred donor naming and the local distance scope as design precedents. No code or data tables reused.
Prior shared-target study tested decay-time matching. This work tests signed onset-delay differences without a disjoint-target comparator.
